                <section class="product--intro">
        <div class="container container-big">

                                                      <div class="field-resume content text-style">
                  <h2>A human adventure that goes beyond the physical challenge</h2>
                </div>

            <div class="row">
                                                              <div class="col-xl-4 col-lg-6 content text-style">
                                                              <div class="field-strengths"><h3>Highlights</h3><ul><li data-list-item-id="ee7b3c95127b1faacc559dac27d1e4b99">A self-sufficient expedition like no other in the world</li><li data-list-item-id="e1fb4f4439a9eb161784d4e6491f42da0">Guided by French-speaking Michael Charavin</li><li data-list-item-id="e8d363169c29e02e58480f08b051b9cae">One of the world's best expedition kiters</li><li data-list-item-id="e95bb3bb0c5cb20f59adeb785127e00bc">Immersion in raw, untamed nature</li><li data-list-item-id="ef5306103c06ba7ac146ee5dd34714f86">A human adventure and a physical challenge</li><li data-list-item-id="edb138a4c94e87cb388aa9cc2d51500aa">H24 personalized weather forecast services and medical hotline</li><li data-list-item-id="ebf00abd937ad91a8075a95c5621abf43">Departure guaranteed from 2 participants and 3 maximum</li></ul></div>                                                              <div class="field-resume"><p>Guided by Michael Charavin, one of today's top expedition kiters, we set off to snowkite across the Greenland icecap from south to north, a journey of almost 1,500 kilometers from Kangerlussuaq to Qaanaaq, or Thule to its friends. No other agency in the world has ever done this. Our expedition should take around 30 days, depending on wind and weather conditions. Once we pass the low-pressure areas of southern Greenland, the katabatic winds of the cap are caught in our sails, and the kilometers are swallowed up with the minimum of effort. You need to be a self-sufficient kiter in all wind and snow conditions. We are organizing a more complete crossing from Narsarsuaq to Qaanaaq: allow 700 kilometers and a fortnight more.</p></div>
                                      </div>

                          </li>
                                                                                                <li class="nav-item">
                            <a class="nav-link" id="tab-ONGLET-PRIX-PERSO-tab" data-toggle="tab" href="#tab-ONGLET-PRIX-PERSO" role="tab" aria-controls="tab-ONGLET-PRIX-PERSO" aria-selected="true">
                              <div class="zone-icon">
                                                                  <i class="icon fontello icon-pictosurmesure"></i>
                                                              </div>
                              <div class="zone-tab-title">
                                <span class="title">Customized expedition</span>
                              </div>
                            </a>
                          </li>
                                                                                                <li class="nav-item">
                            <a class="nav-link" id="tab--tab" data-toggle="tab" href="#tab-" role="tab" aria-controls="tab-" aria-selected="true">
                              <div class="zone-icon">
                                                                  <i class="icon fi flaticon-chat"></i>
                                                              </div>
                              <div class="zone-tab-title">
                                <span class="title">Frequently asked questions</span>
                              </div>
                            </a>
                          </li>
                                                                  </ul>
                                  </div>
                <div class="col-lg-8">
                                      <div class="tab-content content text-style" id="product--tabs-content"><div class="tab-pane fade tab-role--descriptif" id="tab-ONGLET-DESCRIPTIF" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-ONGLET-DESCRIPTIF-tab"><h2 class="tab-title">Overview</h2>

      <div class="field field--descriptif2 field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p><a href="https://youtu.be/csn6DxwFLlo" target="_blank">A short video of our August / September 2020 crossing<u>.</u></a></p><p><iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/csn6DxwFLlo" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen=""></iframe></p><p>We set off from the south of Greenland as logistics are easier and the weather conditions are often better than in the north. Moreover, the east and west katabatic winds are more often southerly than northerly. We thus land at Kangerlussuaq and check our equipment down to the last detail. A helicopter will then drop us at the ice cap at the starting point of the expedition some thirty kilometers further on. With our pulkas weighing 70 kg, we set off for a journey of 1,500 kilometers, in other words probably some thirty days according to wind conditions. </p><p>What is hardest is to get underway in such an ambitious project. This is due to physical, technical and also meteorological reasons in southern Greenland... Hence the importance of setting off slowly.</p><p>But as soon as we start to feel the effect of the katabatic winds, frequently present on this route, our progression becomes sheer magic, as our sails pull us forward effortlessly. The wind will be our guide throughout our journey, and we shall take advantage of all kite skiing opportunities.  With steady light winds we can cover up to 150 kilometers per day. At 30/40 km/h we can cover 300 kilometers in ten hours. But on some days without wind or, on the contrary, in stormy conditions, we shall make no headway at all. An average of 70 kilometers per day seems fairly realistic.</p><p>Our speed of progression will depend solely on the wind and we will need to turn west and leave the ice cap at Qaanaaq (Thule) to reach the small village of Siorapaluk where the Inuits in their dog sleds will be our first signs of civilization... On our way, we will pass the famous Dye 2 American army base, dating from the Cold War, today abandoned.</p><p>The differences in altitude along the route account for the dynamics creating the katabatic winds of the ice cap which, combined with weather conditions, create playing surfaces that are more varied than at first sight.</p><p>This is first and foremost a fantastic human adventure requiring a genuine team spirit and group cohesion. Temperatures can drop to −20 or −30°C and storms can make all progress impossible. There may be no wind for several days running. Patience is then the master word. Such is the key to success of this kind of expedition, which calls for a gradual introduction... acclimatization to the cold, to physical exertion, etc. This is where the know-how and experience of your guide comes into its own.</p></div>
                      </div>
  </div>
<div class="tab-pane fade show active tab-role--daybyday" id="tab-ONGLET-JOUR" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-ONGLET-JOUR-tab"><h2 class="tab-title">Itinerary</h2>

      <div class="field field--jour00 field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 0</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>To make concrete what our day-by-day might look like, we imagined a totally fictional but realistic 30-day expedition. We based it on Dixie's kite expedition of 2014, to which we added elements of our snowkite crossing expedition from west to east in 2019 and then south to north in 2020, as well as our Greenland ski pulka crossing expeditions of 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2023. Then we added a few days of contingency days... The day-by-day that follows is therefore purely illustrative.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--jour01 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAYS 1 &amp; 2: ARRIVAL IN KANGERLUSSUAQ — PREPARATION DAY</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 1</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Arrival at Kangerlussuaq airport. We will spend the rest of the day then the next day making the final preparations. We check our equipment for the last time before our departure.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--transfer-transportation with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Transportation:">Air Greenland flight from Copenhagen to Kangerlussuaq Flight duration</span>
              </span>
                                                                        <span class="field-info field-info--jourrep ">
                <span data-label=""><em>Meals:</em> in homestay</span>
              </span>
                                                                        <span class="field-info field-info--jourheb ">
                <span data-label="">Accommodation: nights in homestay</span>
              </span>
                              </div>
          </div>
      <div class="field field--jour03 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 3: START OF EXPEDITION FROM KANGERLUSSUAQ</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 3</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Early morning departure by helicopter that will drop us on the ice cap. The wind is insufficient to pull us, but we take our kites out anyway to have some fun. We set up our first camp. The temperature is mild and the weather beautiful.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--transfer-transportation with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Transportation:">by helicopter to the starting point of the expedition on the ice cap</span>
              </span>

                <span data-label="Transportation duration:">approximately 45 minutes</span>
              </span>

                <span data-label=""><em>Meals:</em> food rations</span>

                <span data-label="">Accommodation: night in tents</span>
              </span>
                              </div>
          </div>
      <div class="field field--jour04 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 4: ADJUSTING THE KITE SAILS</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 4</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Fog and wind. After walking one hour, we take out our sails, but the wind quickly drops. “We content ourselves with a technical briefing and an adjustment of our sails”.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--average-daily-distance with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Average daily distance:">13 km Activities</span>

              </span>
                              </div>
          </div>
      <div class="field field--jour05 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 5: COLD DAY</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 5</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Cold morning. After a 2-hour wait, as forecast, the sails are set in motion. A long-awaited, magical moment. Using the wind's natural energy is fabulous... We cover a distance that is still too short for sailing, but it is time to get into the swing of things. Camp is set up by 5 p.m.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--distance with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Distance:">47 km Activities</span>
              </span>

                <span data-label="">Accommodation: night in tents</span>
              </span>
                              </div>
          </div>
      <div class="field field--jour06 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 6: FINE WEATHER</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 6</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>A lovely day, ideal for continuing to perfect our kite skiing technique! We cover 60 kilometers.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--number-of-activity-hours with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Number of activity hours:">approximately 5 h Activities</span>

      <div class="field field--jour07 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 7: DISTANCES COVERED ARE INCREASING</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 7</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Thirty minutes’ walking to warm up. The sails then come out of the pulkas and, one by one, swell up with the wind. At 6 p.m. the expedition has covered more than 120 kilometers. Spirits are rising. Indeed, we left five days ago "already" and we have "only" covered 250 kilometers. At this rate we willl need two months to reach Qaanaaq!</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--distance with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Distance:">36 km Activities</span>

      <div class="field field--jour08 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 8: 160 KILOMETERS TODAY</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 8</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Wind and clouds. Snow and wind conditions are excellent and, at the end of the afternoon, the group sets up camp 160 kilometers further on! "That day, we markedly drifted to the north. We rely on the katabatic winds to correct our course. During the day, gusty winds of up to 50 km/h, before falling to light winds in the evening."</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 9</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Magnificent fresh snow fell overnight. It simply sparkles. Steady wind. Nine hours’ snowkiting to cover 210 kilometers.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">

              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 10: BAD WEATHER</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 10</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Winds at more than 50 km/h. Zero visibility. We decide to remain in our tents… What a pleasure to listen to music while tucked cozily into our sleeping bags... And how great it is to be here!</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 11</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>In our tents… we exchange ideas, enjoy the silence, write in our logbooks, sort our photos for the first time…</p></div>

              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 12: MORNING STORM</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 12</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Despite the storm, we try to launch our sails. But the wind is too strong, increasing at midday up to 100 km/h in gusts. The situation is urgent. We have to set up camp in extreme conditions. Impossible to do more than 5 kilometers. The elements are the decision-makers... we need to remain humble to ensure the success of our expedition.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">

              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 13: RETURN OF GOOD WEATHER AND WIND</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 13</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>A good steady easterly wind and 140 kilometers under our belt. The weather worsens in the evening with fog and sleet. But our weather forecaster talks of clear spells and a good wind for tomorrow. We already feel much better!  </p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 14</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Ninety kilometers in fine weather and mild temperatures.</p></div>

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 15</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>A tailwind, fairly light,requiring a technical sail approach. We set up camp at around 6 p.m. In Dixie’s words: "Instead of 'parking' our sail in the air and letting the wind carry us away, we should try to generate more wind."</p></div>

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 16</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Fair settled weather. Conditions are just perfect, what more could we want!</p></div>

              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 17: 260 KILOMETERS COVERED!</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 17</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>We have the impression that the wind is rising continuously and steadily. We achieve our record of 260 kilometers in 9 hours. If we have the same weather conditions tomorrow, we will aim at doing 12 hours!</p></div>

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 18</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>The wind quickly drops late morning and we "only" cover 67 kilometers today.</p></div>

                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>In our tent, we see the barometer rising, thus announcing a low.</p></div>

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 21</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>The wind blows outside. The book we took (having removed its cover to limit weight) is a great way to pass the time.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">

              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 23: LIGHT WIND</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 23</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>We cover 60 kilometers today on our kite skis. The sky has cleared and a weather forecast from the Lyon team announces a fine weather window with a wind blowing steadily at 20 knots from the south-east for the next three days. We feel really good after our forced period of inactivity and are ready to go!</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--distance with-sublabel">

              <h3 class="field-title">DAYS 24 TO 26: UNDER SAIL</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 24</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>These three days are simply magical and allow us to cover 400 kilometers, i.e. 133 kilometers per day. We do not go very fast but we kite 7 hours a day. We are now only 200 kilometers from the finishing point!</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--average-daily-distance with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Average daily distance:">133 km Activities</span>
              </span>
                                                                        <span class="field-info field-info--jourrep ">
                <span data-label=""><em>Meals:</em> food rations</span>
              </span>
                                                                        <span class="field-info field-info--jourheb ">
                <span data-label="">Accommodation: nights in tents</span>
              </span>
                              </div>
          </div>
      <div class="field field--jour27 field--with-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">DAY 27: HEADING WEST</h3>
                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 27</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>We leave the ridge of the ice cap to head west, towards Qaanaaq and Siorapaluk. The north-west wind is not in our favor and we have to weave, that is to say zig zag, to stay on course.</p></div>
                          <div class="field-infos">
                                                            <span class="field-info field-info--distance with-sublabel">
                <span data-label="Distance:">80 km Activities</span>
              </span>
                                                                        <span class="field-info field-info--jourrep ">

                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p><em>Bis repetita</em>. We continue to weave. Two days, very trying for our morale, with a wind easing off, so close from our goal... We are beginning to guess the coastline.</p></div>

                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Thick fog at the start of the day. The wind has veered. In the middle of the afternoon, we begin to make out the coast line. This is probably our last camp. Emotions are running high! We are nearly there!</p></div>

                    <h4 class="field-subtitle">Day 32</h4>
                    <div class="field-paragraph"><p>At midday, we reach Siorapaluk, a small fishing and hunting village. We have made it! The inhabitants welcome us and ask, surprised, where on earth we come from. We spend the night in a homestay reserved especially for us. Festive evening.</p></div>

      <div class="field field--fin-programme field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">END OF EXPEDITION</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>For reasons that cannot be foreseen at this stage, such as unpredictable weather, the physical fitness or lack of fitness of participants or other circumstancess (customs formalities, road conditions, traffic, landslides, force majeure, etc.), your expedition leader may have to adapt the program, if necessary, to ensure the smooth running of your trip. He remains the sole judge and the one who guarantees your safety. Activity times are given as an indication and may vary from one participant to another.</p><p>The itinerary for all our expedition programs, or the ascent program for our high-mountain expeditions, are given here as a guide only. They are flexible enough to adapt to weather conditions with a few contingency days. In any case, you should follow the recommendations of your guide, who may suggest that you cancel your expedition due to weather, safety or physical conditions.</p><p>It is important to remember that this is a truly unsupported expedition, and that anything can happen. Expeditions Unlimited, your expedition leader, your guide or our local teams can in no way be held responsible.</p><p><u>Any costs incurred as a result of a change in the expedition schedule (extra nights' accommodation, extra flights) will be borne by the participants and not by the organizers. "Contingency days" refer to the expedition in the strict sense of the term (base camp/base camp in the mountains, departure point/exit point on a traverse, etc.).</u><br></p><p><u>Any early return of the expedition or of certain members only (early success, abandonment, etc.), generating costs for accommodation, meals, changes to air tickets or other activities not provided for in this program, will be charged in full to the participants.</u><br></p><p><u></u></p></div>

<div class="tab-pane fade tab-role--details" id="tab-ONGLET-TECHNIQUE" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-ONGLET-TECHNIQUE-tab"><h2 class="tab-title">Trip notes</h2>

      <div class="field field--guide field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Guiding</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Your expedition leader is Michael Charavin. Mika is both French-speaking and English-speaking and very experienced in snowkiting, polar environments and in group management (please see above description).</p><p>The leader represents Expeditions Unlimited with the group, our partners and local authorities. He makes the decisions necessary for the smooth running of the expedition. You will have to respect his decisions as well as those taken collectively. Should he be unable to take decisions, Manu would then take the lead. His authority would be preponderant and unavoidable. You would have to respect his decisions.</p><p>If for reasons beyond our control and duly substantiated, Michael Charavin cannot guide the group, then they will be replaced by another experienced polar guiding team. The services would not be modified, the travel conditions would therefore be identical and this change would not constitute a valid reason for cancellation.</p><p>And throughout the program, we will draw on other local skills as needed. Finally, we will have access to a very experienced weather router and a doctor specializing in cold and isolated environments H24.</p><p>For unpredictable reasons at this stage, like adverse weather conditions, insufficient physical condition of participants, insufficient competencies of participants related to the intended activities, your guide may decide to adjust the intended program and/or activities. At all times, his decision will be final on all matters likely to affect the safety and well-being of the trip.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--difficultes field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Difficulty level</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><h3>Level rated: difficult</h3>
<p>This program is aimed at participants in good physical shape, with a significant sport practice, endurance in particular, holding a strong mental to face difficulties that are unforeseen by nature.</p><p>This program is described as difficult, given the distances covered, the isolation, the carrying, and the climatic and environmental conditions. Participants carry the loads in their pulkas, which weigh nearly 70 kg at the start. A very good physical and mental condition is therefore imperative. A good level of kite sailing is a must (see below), and experience of the far north and of mountaineering is naturally a plus. Each participant is responsible for the application of safety rules, equipment and maintenance, setting up camp and preparing meals. As always in this type of project, the key to success is teamwork and team spirit. Participation in the preparation course, the date of which will be specified at a later date, is therefore essential. Last but not least, the Greenlandic government requires a particularly detailed dossier to authorize our expedition. In particular, we will be asked to provide an expedition / trek / sports CV for each participant, enabling us to measure the latter's ability to succeed in the project with a high probability. Under 65, no medical certificate is required.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--niveau-difficulte-technique field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Technical difficulty</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><h3>Level of snowkiting: Autonomous</h3><p>You have a significant experience and knowledge of snowkiting, both in training and in multiple day expeditions. You have developed a solid set of skills. You can assess all the risk factors, before you put a kite in the air. You can fly your kite by feel and know exactly how it will react in all situations so that you can focus on skiing and terrain. You master the “Power Zone” and have a healthy respect for it. You can safely launch, fly and land your kite in all wind and weather conditions. You have a correct understanding of wind and weather as it is important to always monitor what is going on with both. You are comfortable moving in every feasible direction. You know how to control speed with placement of the kite in the wind window and edging of your skis. You know how to select your kite dimension depending upon wind and weather conditions. You kite on all terrain, on level ground or not, on the flats or uphill. You anticipate problems. When something goes wrong, you stay calm and try to think clearly through the situation. You know how to inspect and maintain your gear. If something needs repair, you can fix it. You have set limits for yourself and stay within those limits. Expeditions Unlimited through its trainings and snowkite expeditions can help you progress in your practice so do not hesitate to contact us.</p><p><span></span></p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--com-flight field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Meeting point</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Meeting point is the starting point of expedition (Kangerlussuaq, Narsarsuaq).</p><p>Given the diverse origins of the participants on this trip, international outward and return flights are not included in this package. In most cases, we book flights on your behalf to ensure that the whole group arrives at the destination at the same time. We do not charge any fees for these air bookings. Please do not hesitate to contact us. If you book your own tickets, we will advise you on the ideal flight schedule to enable all participants to arrive within a reduced time frame. At the very least, you need tickets that can be modified. </p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--hebergement field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Accommodations</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>As marked in the program, accommodation is in hotels or in homestays in two to eight bed rooms at the start and finish of the expedition (included in this package for 3 nights at most), then in two-person tents during the expedition. Additional nights, if any, at the start and finish of the expedition could be in tents, in a communal building, in a homestay or hotel, at the guide’s discretion. Overnight stays in Copenhagen or Reykjavik (stopovers) are not covered and must be paid for by the participant.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--repasft field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Meals</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Dinners are taken in homestay at the start and finish of the expedition (included in this package, for 3 dinners at most). During the expedition, meals are prepared beforehand in freeze-dried form. They provide us with all the calories we need for the expedition with priority given to a balanced diet, light weight, and simplicity of preparation. Meals in Copenhagen or Reykjavik (stopovers) are not covered.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--transfert-transport field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Transfers / Transport</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Transfers from/to airport are collective and are ensured by taxis, helicopter, dogsled, sno-cat, etc.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--com-group-size field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Group size</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>The group is composed of 2 to 3 participants maximum. The number of participants is deliberately limited to allow for greater immersion, to avoid embarrassing our hosts, and to develop freedom and flexibility. However, the maximum number may be exceeded if the last person to register wishes to travel with one or more other people. The services will not be modified, and the conditions of the trip will remain the same.</p></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--com-equipement field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Equipment</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><h3>Equipment</h3><p>Personal equipment is not provided. However, a complete list is provided to allow you to check that you are taking what is necessary.</p><p>All logistical equipment is provided, including tents and pulkas, as well as collective equipment such as stoves, white gas, etc.</p><p>Your guide is equipped with a satellite phone, Garmin Inreach and emergency equipment, and a geolocation beacon.</p><p>Other personal equipment is not supplied. A complete list is provided below.</p><p>For reference, we offer technical equipment for rental, for example (please contact us for specific needs):</p><ul><li>Thor Neo Valandre down sleeping bag -30°C: €150 to €200 depending on the rental duration (deposit of €1000, not cashed if paid by cheque)</li><li>Valandre down jacket -30°C: €110 to €140 depending on the rental duration (deposit of €700, not cashed if paid by cheque)</li><li>Valandre down salopettes -30°C: €110 to €140 depending on the rental duration (deposit of €700, not cashed if paid by cheque)</li></ul></div>
                      </div>
      <div class="field field--com-sust field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
              <h3 class="field-title">Our commitments to sustainable development</h3>
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Our commitment to a better planet has been a reality since the beginning of our story but we always need to do more and better. <a href="https://www.secret-planet.com/en/sustainable-development" target="_blank">Please find out more about our charter and our commitments in terms of sustainable development. We have drafted our charter and take action through six themes</a> on which we act as concretely as possible, most often with you: social equity and cultural respect, preservation of water, waste management in expedition, protection of biodiversity, raise public awareness on these subjects and finally, the optimization and recovery of CO<sub>2</sub><span class="redactor-invisible-space"></span> emissions.</p><p>Regarding carbon emissions, most of which are due to air travel, we calculated and communicated in 2018 on the carbon footprint of each of our programs, expressed in tonnes of <span class="redactor-invisible-space">CO<sub>2</sub></span>.</p><p><strong>And in 2022, we have set ourselves a carbon reduction target that we believe is unprecedented in the tourism industry, aiming to reduce the total emissions of our activity by 5% per year, taking 2019 as the reference year</strong> (3,430 tonnes of <span class="redactor-invisible-space">CO<sub>2</sub></span>). This commitment is in line with the trajectory of the Paris climate agreements of 2015, the current benchmark. By 2030, we aim to not exceed 2,160 tons of <span class="redactor-invisible-space">CO<sub>2</sub></span>. In 2024, all Secret
Planet journeys emitted 2,064 tons, well below our maximum limit of
2,940 tons. The ceiling for 2025 is 2,800 tons, and in 2026 it will be
further reduced to 2,660 tons. And so on until 2030. <a href="https://www.secret-planet.com/en/calculations-and-reduction-carbon-emissions" target="_blank">To find out more about all of our calculations and our commitments in terms of reducing our carbon emissions</a>.</p><p><strong>In addition, since 2019, we have been encouraging you when you book for your journey to contribute with a donation to an independent NGO, among the two we have selected that share the commitments made in our charter</strong>. We matched the amount of this donation to this program's carbon footprint. Thus, the journey you are considering generates<strong> 2,55 tons of <span class="redactor-invisible-space">CO<sub>2</sub></span>, which corresponds to a 100% donation of <strong>€</strong>77 </strong>for an estimated value today of €30 per tonne of <span class="redactor-invisible-space">CO<sub>2</sub></span>. This donation remains of course optional and you can decide to give between nothing and 100% of this amount. <strong>Since 2019, including covid years of 2020 and 2021, we have been able to collect thanks to you nearly €5,500 for these associations.</strong></p><p>Please do not hesitate to come back to us with any questions you might have regarding this carbon footprint mechanism, our other sustainable développement commitments or even to share with us your experience through a chat or a mail at <a href="mailto:developpement-durable@secret-planet.com">contact@secret-planet.com</a>.</p></div>
                      </div>
  </div>
<div class="tab-pane fade tab-role--guide" id="tab-ONGLET-5" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-ONGLET-5-tab"><h2 class="tab-title">Michael Charavin, kiter and  polar guide</h2>

      <div class="field field--accompagnateur field--without-infos field--with-paragraph">
                          <div class="field-paragraph"><p>Born in 1970, Mika has been a state certified guide since 1999, snowkite instructor, guide in the polar regions since 2003 and is part of the IPGA – <em>International Polar Guide Association</em>, which brings together the best polar guides in world. He has been snowkiting in boreal and arctic regions for 20 years and has traveled more than 15,000 kilometers on expeditions in this way. He is one of the few polar guides specializing in this practice.</p><p>He is one of the very first to have crossed Greenland by snowkite from south to north-west (2,300 km in 2008) then to have completed a circumnavigation of the Greenland ice sheet (5,067 km in 2014). He becomes on this occasion (and until 2019) the author of the longest trip ever undertaken on skis and independently. It is also innovative in its way of practicing snowkiting in the mountains (the most complex playground there is for this activity), by combining ascents of summits and crossings of massifs.</p><p>Called up in 1994, he spent fourteen months as a technical aid volunteer in the French southern and Antarctic Lands, on the Kerguelen archipelago, where he contributed to various eco-ethological studies and the restoration of subantarctic ecosystems. Then in 1996-1997, he crossed 8,000 kilometers by mountain bike through the highlands of southern Latin America, from the Bolivian Amazon to Tierra del Fuego, passing through the Altiplano, the deserts of Sud-Lipez and the Puna of Atacama, Patagonia...</p><p>From 1999, his taste for the wilderness, isolated, austere and cold regions, became even more refined: he turned resolutely towards the Nordic regions, and invested his energy in carrying out committed and stripped down ski expeditions: 1,800 kilometers and four months of itinerant skiing across Scandinavia (from south to north) in 2000; various raids and several hundred kilometers in the central, western and southern regions of Spitsbergen in 2001 and 2002; attempted east-west crossing of Greenland in 2003...</p><p>Always driven by a deep passion for the great ski crossings of the polar or subpolar regions, he nevertheless modified his approach to these environments from 2006: to the rigor necessary for the logistical, technical and mental preparation of such expeditions, he now wishes add performance and technicality, key notions, according to him, in the realization of great raids, in particular in the extreme environments which are the large ice caps. It is also a way of reintroducing a playful dimension into an activity that is fundamentally devoid of it...</p><p>In total, he has supervised numerous trips, on skis, on foot or by sea kayak, to Greenland, Iceland, Norway, Spitsbergen, Alaska and the French southern lands...</p></div>
                      </div>
  </div>

<div class="tab-pane fade tab-role--generic" id="tab-ONGLET-PRIX-PERSO" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-ONGLET-PRIX-PERSO-tab"><h2 class="tab-title">Customized expedition</h2><div class="customizable-form"><div class="text-intro text-intro--before-customizable"><h3>Bring your expedition to life—designed to match your ambition.</h3>
<p><strong>Does one of our existing expedition almost align with your objective?</strong> We can tailor it precisely: adjust the duration, refine the level of commitment, integrate specific goals (scientific, athletic, audiovisual production), adapt the logistics, or strengthen supervision and safety measures. This approach is built on proven terrain in order to create an expedition fully aligned with your goals.</p>
<p><strong>Is your project unique and unlike anything that we currently offer?</strong> We design fully custom expeditions. This is no longer about adapting an existing program, but about building a complete project based on your constraints, your level of engagement, your objectives, and the realities of the field. Remote environments, extreme conditions, complex logistics, or specific projects (exploration, filming, scientific missions, personal challenges): every expedition is designed with precision and uncompromising standards.</p>
<p>For over 15 years, Expeditions Unlimited has been designing and operating expeditions worldwide—across all regions, environments, and activities—for individuals and corporate projects alike. Our field expertise ensures reliable systems, robust logistics, and controlled management of demanding environments.</p>
<p>Because every project is unique, our commitment is clear: to support you in designing and executing a safe, fully realized expedition that truly reflects your ambition.</p>
<p><a href="/en/customized-expeditions" data-entity-type="node" data-entity-uuid="f3af777f-c612-4c4f-976b-b9bed97c574d" data-entity-substitution="canonical" title="Customized expeditions">Learn more about our custom expedition approach.</a></p>
<h3>Tell us about your project</h3>
<p>A few details are enough to get started. One of our experts will contact you within 48 hours to better understand your needs and propose a tailored approach.</p>
</div>

<div class="tab-pane fade tab-role--faq" id="tab-" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab--tab"><h2 class="tab-title">Frequently asked questions</h2>
            <div class="field field--name-field-faq field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden text-style field__item">
              <div id="faqs-37638" class="paragraph paragraph--type--faqs paragraph--view-mode--default faqs">

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item" open>
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What snowkite level is required for this crossing?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>Full autonomous mastery of snowkite in extreme conditions is required: safe landing in all wind situations, emergency management, progression over varied terrain, and advanced meteorological awareness. Prior experience including advanced training courses and multi-day self-sufficient expeditions is necessary before applying. Candidates without polar snowkite background must demonstrate solid knowledge of katabatic winds and Arctic conditions.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What physical fitness level is expected?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The program demands elite athletic fitness with exceptional cardiovascular and muscular endurance. Participants must be able to pull a 70 kg pulka over long distances in extreme cold and high winds, day after day for a month. Targeted physical preparation started several months in advance is strongly advised.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What documents and prerequisites are required at registration?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>A detailed expedition CV listing snowkite outings and polar experience is required at registration. A full medical assessment is also mandatory, validated during the pre-departure appointment with Ifremmont. Candidate selection is rigorous given the expedition's commitment level and the strictly limited group of 2 to 3 participants.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">Is the pre-departure preparation mandatory and what does it involve?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>Two pre-departure sessions, each lasting one to two days, are held between December and February for participants registered more than six months in advance. One focuses on technical preparation covering equipment and expedition tactics; the other is a medical and physiological assessment conducted with Ifremmont. These sessions are an integral part of the program, included in the price.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">How is the progression structured across the 1,500 km ice cap?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The expedition begins with a helicopter transfer from Kangerlussuaq to the starting point on the ice cap, reaching altitudes where katabatic winds are reliably exploitable. The northward crossing toward Qaanaaq/Siorapaluk is undertaken in full self-sufficiency, with daily distances varying widely depending on conditions, from zero to over 200 km. The return to civilization involves a boat and then a flight from Qaanaaq.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">How are katabatic winds used as the main driving force?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>Katabatic winds, which flow down from the elevated central plateau and blow northward, are most reliable and powerful in April and May, which is why the expedition departs during this period. A dedicated weather router monitors wind systems continuously to support day-by-day tactical decisions. The south-to-north direction is specifically designed to harness these winds in the most favorable direction for progression.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">How are weather holds and reserve days managed?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The 35-day program includes built-in reserve days to absorb storm periods or unusable wind conditions. During holds, participants remain camped autonomously on the ice sheet. If delays exceed the planned reserve days, additional costs may apply, which should be factored into the overall trip budget.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What technically characterizes the Greenland ice cap for a kiter?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The ice sheet is an elevated glacial plateau, typically between 1500 m and 2000 m above sea level, exposed to very low temperatures and potentially violent winds even in April. The surface alternates between smooth sections favorable to kiting and areas of sastrugi (hardened snow ridges that disrupt progress and demand physical effort). Total isolation, hundreds of kilometers from any outside assistance, is the most committed aspect of this terrain.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What are the most demanding sections of the crossing?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The first days on the ice cap, departing from the south, often bring less stable wind conditions before reaching reliable katabatic zones. Central sections can feature significant sastrugi fields that slow progress and increase physical fatigue. Managing long waiting days in full self-sufficiency, with no possibility of immediate evacuation, is the most psychologically demanding aspect of the program.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">Why cross from south to north rather than the reverse?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The south-to-north direction is determined by the physics of katabatic winds, which flow down from the elevated ice sheet and blow northward, serving as the main engine of snowkite progression. Attempting the crossing in reverse would mean working against the prevailing winds, making the expedition technically incompatible with snowkite on this route. The arrival at Qaanaaq/Siorapaluk, an Inuit village in northern Greenland, also provides a uniquely human and cultural conclusion to the journey.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What is the guide's role and how does the group operate in the field?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>Guide Michael Charavin, IPGA certified and specialized in polar snowkite expeditions, handles day-to-day technical leadership, tactical decisions on progression or waiting, and management of critical situations. The group is intentionally capped at 2 to 3 participants to maintain team cohesion and allow progression suited to each individual. The ratio of 1 guide to 2 or 3 participants ensures personalized support throughout.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What medical and safety systems are in place during the expedition?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>24/7 access to a specialized medical hotline (Ifremmont) is included in the program. Each participant carries a Garmin InReach GPS device and a satellite phone for emergency communication and position tracking. A professional weather router monitors conditions continuously throughout the expedition.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What does the program include and what remains the participant's responsibility?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>The program covers field transfers, gite accommodation at departure and arrival (up to 3 nights), freeze-dried meals throughout the crossing plus 3 gite dinners, all collective equipment (tents, pulkas, stoves, fuel, satellite phone, Garmin InReach), pre-departure preparation sessions, and Ifremmont medical support. International flights, personal cold-weather gear (available to rent locally), supplementary insurance, and any costs arising from weather delays remain the participant's responsibility.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">How does this crossing differ from other polar ski expeditions or other Greenland crossings?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>Unlike classic Greenland ski crossings done by manhauling or hand-pulled pulka, snowkite uses wind power as its engine, enabling vastly greater daily distances on favorable days. The south-to-north route covering 1,500 km is longer and more ambitious than the classic east-to-west crossing of approximately 570 km. The small group format, the arrival at Siorapaluk, and contact with Inuit communities give this route an authenticity that is hard to find elsewhere.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      <details class="paragraph paragraph--type--faq paragraph--view-mode--default faq-item">
          <summary class="faq-item__summary">
        <h3 class="faq-item__question">What progression is recommended before applying for this expedition?</h3>
      </summary>
        <div class="faq-item__answer text-style">

            <div class="field field--name-field-text field--type-text-long field--label-hidden text-style field__item"><p>No single preparatory program is prescribed, but candidates must have accumulated solid snowkite experience including advanced courses and multi-day expeditions in real winter conditions, ideally in Arctic or subarctic environments. Familiarity with polar terrain (Scandinavia, Iceland, the Canadian Arctic) is valued so that Greenland does not become a first polar experience. For those building toward this level, other polar programs in the catalog provide natural stepping stones.</p>
</div>

    </div>
  </details>

      </div>

</div>
      </div>
</div>
                                  </div>
              </div>
            </section>
          </div>
